newsitem.title: FRANCE: French artists fight far-right mayor over theatre.
newsitem.headline: French artists fight far-right mayor over theatre.

text.p: Several hundred singers, actors, filmmakers and other artists protested in Toulon in southern France on Thursday against an order by the far-right National Front mayor to sack a local theatre director.

The artists travelled overnight aboard a so-called "Freedom Train" to the Mediterranean port, one of four southern towns held by the anti-immigration Front, to fight the sacking of theatre director Gerard Paquet by mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier.
"I cannot accept the diktat of a party...What is happening is typical of a totalitarian or fascistic state attacking culture and freedom," rock star Jacques Higelin told reporters.

The artists, including film directors Claude Chabrol and Bertrand Tavernier, comedian Guy Bedos and actor Roger Hanin, attended a court hearing on Paquet's sacking and planned to march through the town.

The hearing began in a tense atmosphere but shortly afterwards was adjourned until March 27 at the request of Le Chevallier, who argued that the board running the theatre might appoint a successor to Paquet on Friday.

Laywers for the theatre and cultural centre at Chateauvallon said Paquet's sacking was illegal and denounced what they called a game played by Le Chevallier, regional prefect (government representative) Jean-Charles Marchiani, and Henri Nespoulous, appointed administrator of the centre.
Le Chevallier has said he would not let the artists protest at the centre. Paquet, after a series of clashes, was sacked for failure to get mayoral approval for printing the programme for 1997.

Chateauvallon became a symbol of opposition to the Front when Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy and writers protested there late last year against Le Chevallier's ban on a tribute to Jewish writer Marek Halter.

Several of the filmmakers present in Toulon had sparred on Wednesday with a government minister, urging people to disobey hardline anti-immigration laws as he invited the directors to spend a month in a run-down suburb to get to grips with reality.

More than 60 directors, including Tavernier and Mathieu Kassowitz, have urged civil disobedience against a law requiring French citizens to report the arrival and departure of foreigners staying at their home.
They also expressed concern at the Front's victory in a local election in the southern town of Vitrolles at the weekend.
There are about five million foreign nationals in France including about a million illegal entrants, most of them from developing countries.
